output.report_titles: Yemen's Economic Outlook- Fall 2016 (2016); Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2016 (2016); Yemen's Economic Outlook- April 2017 (2017); Yemen's Economic Outlook - October 2017 (2017); Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2022: Clearing Skies Over Yemen? (2022); Yemen Economic Monitor, Fall 2023: Navigating Increased Hardship and Growing Fragmentation (2023); Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2024: Navigating Increased Hardship and Growing Fragmentation (2024); Yemen Economic Monitor, Fall 2024: Confronting Escalating Challenges (2024); Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2025 (2025); Yemen Economic Monitor, November 2025 (2025); MENA Economic Monitor, October 2015: Inequality, Uprisings, and Conflict in the Arab World (Yemen Country Note) (2015); Yemen's Economic Outlook - October 2018 (2018); Yemen's Economic Update - April 2019 (2019); Yemen's Economic Update — October 2019 (2019); Yemen Monthly Economic Update - December 2019 (2019); Yemen's Economic Update — October 2020 (2020); Yemen Monthly Economic Update - January 2020 (2020); Yemen's Economic Update - April 2021 (2021); Yemen's Economic Update - October 2021 (2021); Yemen Economic Monitor: Peace on the Horizon? - Fall 2023 (2023); Yemen Economic Monitor: Navigating Increased Hardship and Growing Fragmentation - Spring 2024 (2024); Yemen Economic Monitor: Confronting Escalating Challenges - Fall 2024 (2024); Yemen Economic Monitor: Persistent Fragility amid Rising Risks - Spring 2025 (2025); Yemen Economic Outlook - Spring 2018 (2018); Yemen Monthly Economic Update- February 2020 (2020); Yemen Monthly Economic Update- March 2020 (2020); Yemen Monthly Economic Update- May 2020 (2020); Yemen Country Economic Memorandum 2022: Glimmers of Hope in Dark Times (2022)
output.key_findings:
• Yemen's Economic Outlook- Fall 2016 (2016):
• Real GDP projected to contract further in 2016 by some 4%.
• Inflation would decline to single digits.
• Fiscal and external current account deficits likely to edge higher.
• Conflict has led to a catastrophic humanitarian situation.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2016 (2016):
• The economy has contracted sharply. Official reporting suggests that the GDP contracted in 2015 by approximately 28%.
• The escalating conflict since March 2015 has led to a catastrophic humanitarian situation.
• The 2016 budget anticipates fiscal consolidation and assumes an average oil price of $35 p/b.
• Real GDP growth is projected at 3.4% in 2016.
• Inflation is projected at 4.8% in 2016.

• Yemen's Economic Outlook- April 2017 (2017):
• Yemen’s GDP contracted since 2015 by about 40%, cumulatively.
• Central Bank became dysfunctional in late 2016.
• UN launched a humanitarian appeal (US$2.1 billion) for helping the 8 million Yemenis suffering from rising food insecurity.
• If peace is restored by mid-2017, the fiscal deficit is estimated to be halved, to 6% of GDP.

• Yemen's Economic Outlook - October 2017 (2017):
• Yemen’s GDP contracted by about 37.5 percent cumulatively since 2015.
• FAO estimates that over 7 million people are at risk of famine in 2017.
• Cholera outbreaks are ravaging the country with nearly 450,000 suspected cases.
• Approximately 40 percent of households reported to have lost their primary income source.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2022: Clearing Skies Over Yemen? (2022):
• Real GDP growth estimated at 1.5% in 2021.
• Real GDP per capita plummeted by 58% since 2015.
• Exchange rate spread between Northern and Southern YER widened in 2021.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Fall 2023: Navigating Increased Hardship and Growing Fragmentation (2023):
• Real GDP projected to contract by 0.5% in 2023.
• Inflation expected to be 15% in 2023.
• Remittances estimated at $3.5 billion annually.
• Over 21.6 million people in need of humanitarian assistance.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2024: Navigating Increased Hardship and Growing Fragmentation (2024):
• Real GDP projected to contract by 1.0% in 2024.
• Inflation expected to be 12% in 2024.
• 80% of the population lives below the poverty line.
• 17 million people facing high levels of acute food insecurity.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Fall 2024: Confronting Escalating Challenges (2024):
• Real GDP projected to contract by 1.0% in 2024.
• Inflation expected to be 12% in 2024.
• Highlights impact of escalating regional tensions on the economy.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, Spring 2025 (2025):
• Real GDP is projected to shrink by 1.5% in 2025.
• Currency pressures, declining aid, and fiscal fragmentation hinder economic recovery.

• Yemen Economic Monitor, November 2025 (2025):
• Provides an update on key economic developments and policies over the past six months.
• Presents findings on the impact of the conflict on specific sectors.

• MENA Economic Monitor, October 2015: Inequality, Uprisings, and Conflict in the Arab World (Yemen Country Note) (2015):
• The economy is likely to contract substantially in 2015. Pre-March estimates suggested a 4% GDP contraction in 2015.
• Oil and gas exports dropped by about 96% in Q2 2015 compared to the year before.
• Annual inflation is expected to increase to double digits in 2015 (was 9% in 2014).
• 21 million people were in need of humanitarian assistance (including 9.9 million children).
• The Social Welfare Fund (SWF) could not disburse financial assistance to its 1.5 million household beneficiaries since December 2014.

• Yemen's Economic Outlook - October 2018 (2018):
• Cumulative economic contraction since March 2015 amounts to approximately 50%.
• GDP reduction estimated at 2.6% in 2018 (compared to 5.9% in 2017).
• If violence is contained by late 2018, GDP is projected to begin to recover in 2019 with double-digit growth.
• Conflict-related adverse economic impacts and distortions show equally negative impact for the supply response and demand side.

• Yemen's Economic Update - April 2019 (2019):
• GDP contracted by an accumulated 39% since the end of 2014.
• If violence is contained by mid-2019, GDP is projected to recover in the second half of the year with a double-digit growth rate.
• Over three-quarters of the population in 2019 are living below US$3.20 PPP a day.
• Approximately half of the population is living below US$1.90 PPP a day.

• Yemen's Economic Update — October 2019 (2019):
• GDP growth turned into positive territory in 2018, arresting a cumulative output contraction of over 40% during 2014-17.
• The economy could grow by 2-2.5% a year over the next 2 years (2020-2021).
• Macroeconomic stabilization supported by balance of payments assistance from Saudi Arabia and gradual recovery of oil and gas production.
• Saudi Arabian deposit is projected to be exhausted by end-2019.

• Yemen Monthly Economic Update - December 2019 (2019):
• Economy was projected to grow at around 2% in 2019, underpinned by a gradual recovery in the oil sector, resumption of gas production, and relative macroeconomic stability.
• Official estimates suggest Yemen exported about 6.7 million barrels of crude oil during the first half of 2019.
• The oil sector continued to recover gradually throughout the year but the production target for 2019 was likely missed.

• Yemen's Economic Update — October 2020 (2020):
• Economic conditions are deteriorating rapidly, driven by a drop in oil exports, downsizing of humanitarian support, and devastating torrential rains and flash floods.
• Socio-economic conditions deteriorated further in 2020, affected by low global oil prices, the economic fallout of COVID-19, and weak public infrastructure.
• Fragmentation of institutional capacity (especially of the Central Bank of Yemen, CBY) and divergent policy decisions between areas of control compound the crisis.

• Yemen Monthly Economic Update - January 2020 (2020):
• In January 2020, the economy was projected to grow at around 2% in 2019.
• The de facto authorities in Sana'a introduced new currency measures that triggered a sharp depreciation of the rial in Aden.
• A recovery in oil production is expected to raise exports and fiscal accounts, with a target to increase the country's oil export capacity to about 80 thousand barrels per day in the first quarter of 2020.
• Sources suggest that as of end-January commercial banks in Sana'a were charging up to 17% for processing cash transfers from the areas controlled by the government in Aden.

• Yemen's Economic Update - April 2021 (2021):
• The economy is estimated to have shrunk by 8.5% in 2020.
• The value of the Yemeni rial continues to depreciate, driving large increases in food prices and pushing more people into extreme poverty.
• The IMF General SDR allocation of $665 million in August 2021 is expected to ease pressures on the balance of payments and foreign exchange market.
• Real GDP growth is projected to recover to 2% in 2021, up from -8.5% in 2020.
• Inflation (CPI) is projected to be 45.0% in 2021, up from 35.0% in 2020.
• Current Account Balance (% of GDP) is projected to be -8.8% in 2021, up from -5.2% in 2020.

• Yemen's Economic Update - October 2021 (2021):
• The economy is estimated to have shrunk by 8.5% in 2020.
• The value of the Yemeni riyal continues to depreciate to new historic lows, driving large increases in food prices and pushing more people into extreme poverty.
• Output is expected to further contract by 2% in 2021 due to the slow recovery in oil production and export capacity and the declining humanitarian funding.
• The macroeconomic policy environment remains complicated by the ongoing conflict, high dependence on imports, and the weakening of the currency.

• Yemen Economic Outlook - Spring 2018 (2018):
• The violent conflict has caused a dramatic deterioration of the economic and social conditions.
• Nearly four-fifths (80%) of the population are living below US$3.20 a day PPP.
• UNOCHA estimates that almost 9 million Yemenis are facing various forms of food insecurity at level 3 or 4.
• Output has contracted sharply, and household incomes are declining.

• Yemen Monthly Economic Update- February 2020 (2020):
• Economic conditions remained relatively calm in February, and internet connectivity was restored after a month-long severe outage.
• Crude oil production grew by about 38% in 2019 to 17.5 million barrels (from 12.7 million in 2018), but export proceeds declined due to lower global oil prices.
• The Yemeni rial remained broadly stable in the south (YR 650 - 665 per US dollar) and the north (YR 597 per US dollar) during February 2020.
• The acceptance of e-rial remains limited, only used for limited expenses like water, electricity, and mobile phone services.

• Yemen Monthly Economic Update- March 2020 (2020):
• Yemen's conflict entered its sixth year in March 2020.
• Declining food stocks, sharply rising food prices, and draining foreign reserves point to a looming food crisis.
• The volume of food imports via Hodeidah and Saleef ports fell since October 2019, with March 2020 volume at only 66% of the 2019 monthly average.
• The national average cost of Minimum Food Basket (MFB) increased by around 3% in February 2020, reaching YR 38,758 (about US$58).
• The exchange rate remained stable in the south (YR 657-660 per US dollar) and the north (YR 600 per US dollar) due to reduced demand for foreign currency (COVID-19 related) and financial surveillance.

• Yemen Monthly Economic Update- May 2020 (2020):
• The World Bank projects a 5% contraction in real GDP in 2020.
• Inflation is projected to be 35% in 2020.
• The current account deficit is projected to widen to 5.2% of GDP in 2020.
• The Yemeni rial depreciated by 12% in the south (Aden) since the beginning of the year.
• The exchange rate gap between the north and south widened to 100 YR per US dollar.
• Remittances are projected to fall by 10% in 2020.

• Yemen Country Economic Memorandum 2022: Glimmers of Hope in Dark Times (2022):
• The report, published in April 2023, serves as the main economic update for the latter half of 2022, in place of a formal Fall 2022 Economic Monitor.
• Yemen’s economy has been shattered by eight years of conflict, leading to a cumulative 50% contraction in GDP between 2015 and 2022.
• The conflict has created a fragmented political and economic landscape, with competing authorities and a bifurcated monetary policy.
• The private sector has shown remarkable resilience, adapting to the challenging environment and continuing to provide essential goods and services.
• The report outlines four potential scenarios for Yemen's future through 2030, ranging from a continuation of the status quo to an "imperfect peace" with enhanced recovery.
• Key policy recommendations include restoring macroeconomic stability, boosting productivity growth, and improving transparency and data availability.

output.report_titles: Yemen: Concluding Statement of the 2025 IMF Article IV Mission (2025); Republic of Yemen: 2014 Article IV Consultation and Request for a Three-Year Arrangement Under the Extended Credit Facility-Staff Report; Press Release; and Statement by the Executive Director for the Republic of Yemen (2014); The Republic of Yemen: 2013 Article IV Consultation (2013); Republic of Yemen: 2007 Article IV Consultation: Staff Report; Staff Supplements; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Executive Director for the Republic of Yemen (2007); Republic of Yemen: Staff Report for the 2004 Article IV Consultation (2004)
output.key_findings:
* Real GDP contracted by approximately 27% over the past decade (2025 report).
* Inflation hit 27% in 2024, rising above 35% year-on-year by July 2025 (2025 report).
* Government revenues declined from 22.5% of GDP in 2014 to below 12% in 2024 (2025 report).
* Oil production declined by 5.9% in 2004 due to diminishing recovery from aging fields (2004 report).
* Non-oil growth was 6% in 2006, offsetting an 8% decline in oil production (2007 report).
* Real GDP grew by 2.4% in 2012, after contracting by more than 12% in 2011 (2013 report).
* Public debt surged to over 100% of IRG GDP by 2024 (2025 report).
* Saudi financial support totaled about $2 billion over 2023–24 (2025 report).

* In 2017, 18.8 million people were in need of humanitarian assistance, with 10.3 million in acute need.
* The 2018 HRP required US$ 2.96 billion to assist 13.1 million people out of 22.2 million in need.
* By 2019, the number of people in need had risen to 24.4 million, with 14 million in acute need.
* The 2022 HRP sought US$ 4.27 billion to assist 17.3 million people out of 23.4 million in need.
* The 2023 HRP required US$ 4.3 billion to reach 17.3 million people out of 21.6 million in need.
* The 2024 HRP required US$ 2.7 billion to assist 11.8 million people out of 18.2 million in need.
* The 2025 HNRP projected 19.5 million people in need of humanitarian assistance and protection services.

output.key_findings:
*   In 2024, 800 solar-powered streetlights were installed and 4 public gardens rehabilitated for community safety.
*   691,300 people indirectly benefited from legal empowerment initiatives in districts.
*   27,593 community members benefited from 70 community safety solutions.
*   In 2022, approximately 4.5 million people were internally displaced, and 17 million people faced crisis-level or worse acute food insecurity in Q4 2023.
*   In 2021, 23.4 million people required humanitarian assistance, with 12.9 million facing extreme or catastrophic severity of living standards.
*   In 2021, more than 25 million Yemenis were food insecure, including 7.3 million one step away from famine.
*   In 2020, a comprehensive damage assessment of two Liebherr cranes in the Port of Hodeida was successfully undertaken, and the rehabilitated Training Center in the Port of Hodeida was completed and handed over.
*   In 2019, a comprehensive damage assessment of the Ports of Hodeidah, Salif, and Ras Issa was undertaken, and 81% of PSF staff were recruited.

* The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) indicators showed normal situation for wheat flour, vegetable oil and red beans, while sugar was on a crisis status. The cost of the minimum food basket stabilized at normal level.
* Prices of food and fuel commodities further declined in August but still remain significantly higher than the pre-crisis levels.
* The cost of the minimum food basket reduced by 9.5% between July and August 2016 but is still 19.5% higher than the pre-crisis level.
* The black market exchange rate of the Yemen Riyal (YER) in August ranged from 295 to 315 per one US Dollar.
* The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) indicators showed normal situation for vegetable oil and red beans, wheat flour at alert status, and sugar on crisis.
* Food prices decreased as post-Ramadan demand declined, yet the minimum food basket cost was 26% higher than pre-crisis level and 13% higher than in April 2016.
* The parallel market rate of the Yemen Riyal (YER) was 283 YER/US$ in July 2016 against an official rate of 250 YER/US$.
* Most of the food commodities were still on Alert status according to ALPS indicators.
* Food commodities availability in June 2016 was considerably worse than May, while fuel commodities were still scarcely available.
* The national sugar market was on crisis, while vegetable oil, red beans and wheat flour were on stress according to ALPS methodology. The basic food basket cost was on stress.
* The total public debt to Gross Domestic Product went up to 94.4%.
* Limited availability of foreign currency pushed the parallel exchange rate up to 300 YER for 1 USD in May 2016.
* Food commodity prices were constantly rising, leading to an increase in the monthly cost of the basic food basket.
* The national red beans market was on crisis, while vegetable oil was on stress and sugar.

output.key_findings:
* Yemen's real GDP is projected to contract by **1.5 percent** in 2025, with a decline in nominal GDP per capita expected to be even more severe, at **19 percent**.
* The economy shrank by **54 percent** between 2015 and 2023.
* The fiscal deficit of the Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) increased to **3.9 percent** of GDP in 2023 due to the reduction in oil exports.
* **74 percent** of the population was below the national poverty line in 2022.
* **18.2 million** people rely on humanitarian assistance, and **15.3 million** people urgently require support in accessing clean water and basic sanitation.
* **62 percent** of households reported inadequate food consumption in July 2024, a **24 percent** increase in IRG-controlled areas and **30 percent** in Houthi-controlled areas compared to the previous year.
* **19 percent** of households have resorted to child labor or dangerous work to survive.
* A child born in Yemen is estimated to be only **37 percent** as productive as they could be if they enjoyed complete education and full health (2020 Human Capital Index).
* The school-age group is expected to expand by **3.84 million** by 2030.

Political and security situation remained fragile, and poverty/unemployment were widespread.
